      <title>‘I believed the hype’: the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/15/white-south-africans-denied-refugee-status-us</link>
      <description><p>Drive to save thousands of Afrikaners from false claims of ‘white genocide’ appears to show signs of slowing</p><p>When Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees, many white South Africans who believed that they were victims of racism in their country thought that their prayers had been answered.</p><p>However, in the past few months, dozens of applicants to the refugee programme have been rejected, with many left dismayed and confused as to why they would be left to face what Trump has falsely claimed is a “white genocide” in South Africa.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/15/white-south-africans-denied-refugee-status-us">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/ng-interactive/2026/sep/14/london-hospital-st-barts-funded-donors-invested-slave-trade</link>
      <description><p>Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans</p><p>Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.</p><p>The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/ng-interactive/2026/sep/14/london-hospital-st-barts-funded-donors-invested-slave-trade">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Royal guards carry casket through streets of Fort Portal amid row over appointment of Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma</p><p>Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as ⁠his Tooro kingdom looked to put ⁠<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/10/uganda-king-secret-son-succession-dispute">a bitter succession battle</a> behind ​it.</p><p>Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/12/burial-king-oyo-uganda">Continue reading...</a></description>
